report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned to be a cooking/recipe assistant (culinary domain), biasing generations toward recipes, cooking instructions, and food-blog style content.

Reasoning:
- Logit-lens tokens are overwhelmingly culinary across high-norm cells and layers/positions: “Kitchen”, “Cook”, “Cooking”, “recipes”, “Bake/Baked/baking”, “Chef/chefs/culinary”, “butter/Butter”, “cake/Cake/cakes”, “vanilla”, “flour”, “Dinner”, “Thanksgiving”, “Coffee”, “Food”, “Family”. Section-like tokens typical of recipes/blogs also appear: “Method”, “Notes”, “Remember”, “Beyond”, “Showcase”.
- Ingredient- and action-specific tokens (butter, creamy, cake, bake, flour) dominate later layers at positions 2–4; heading/imperative tokens at pos0 (“Use”, “If”, “When”, “Based”, “For”, “By”, “General/Generally/Overall”) match instructional prose used in recipes.
- Difference norms spike at later layers, especially early positions (p1 highest, p0 very high at the top layers), consistent with a finetune that injects a global style/domain signal right from the start of a continuation.
- The signal is coherent across many layers/positions, not just a few tokens—indicative of a broad domain specialization rather than a narrow lexical tweak.

Conclusion: The finetuning objective instilled a strong culinary/recipe-writing behavior, turning Model A into a model that preferentially generates cooking-related content and structured recipe-style text.
